Workspaces · 50+ tools
Ten workspaces · One app · 50+ tools

Delete the pile. Keep the day.

Most drivers run one working day across a phone full of apps — GPS in one, loads in another, fuel prices in a third, hours in a fourth, pay chased through a spreadsheet and a folder of PDFs. Every login is a seam, and money falls through seams. STONEMILES folds all of it into one workspace with ten doors — ten workspaces on your Today screen, each one opening straight onto its tools, each one named at its home so you always know where you are. 50+ tools, one home, nothing living in two places — the load you book is the load the GPS runs, the trip the hours clock seals, and the pay the settlement gets checked against. That is the whole point: throw the old apps away.

01Find it · Book it · Haul it

Loads

The work starts here. The loadboard, your next-load suggestions, your booked loads and the sealed Load Tracker live behind one door — broker sends, desk assignments and board loads all land in the same place, so the load you take is the load every other workspace already knows about. And booking one just got faster: snap or upload the rate confirmation and the load fills in for your check-off before it seals — shipper, receiver, dates and rate read off the paper, not typed in by thumb. Manual entry is always right there if the read misses anything.

Replaces: the loadboard app, the broker-text thread, the notebook of load numbers.
02Truck GPS · Cab Mode · Hours clock

Drive

The road, run from one screen. Truck-legal GPS that knows your height, weight and trailer, a glanceable Cab Mode built for one look and one tap, and your hours-of-service clock riding right beside the route — so the miles, the alerts and the time you have left are never in different apps arguing with each other.

Replaces: the car GPS, the separate logbook app, the second phone on the dash.
03Plan the run: routes, parking, stops

Planner

A run planned before the wheels turn beats a run rescued at midnight. Compare routes, line up parking and stops against your real hours clock, and see the weather on the road at the hour you will actually be there — the day laid out while there is still time to change it.

Replaces: the parking app, the weather guesswork, the “we’ll figure it out” stop hunt.
04Cheapest stops · True cost

Fuel

The pump price is not the price. Fuel ranks the stops on your actual route by what a gallon truly costs you, keeps your fuel log and builds the IFTA picture as you drive — so the cheapest stop is the one that is cheapest for your run, not the loudest sign on the interstate.

Replaces: the fuel-price app, the receipt envelope, the quarter-end IFTA scramble.
05Earned · Owed · Checked

Pay

What you earned, who still owes you, and whether the settlement that landed actually matches the work — in one place. Your revenue per mile sits up front at the top of Pay, figured from your sealed loads, so the number that decides whether a run was worth it is the first thing you see — not a spreadsheet you build later. Pay Book, who-owes-me, invoices and profit & loss sit behind this door, the invoice draft from your delivery POD is already waiting here, and now every settlement gets checked automatically against your sealed loads the moment you log it. And for 1099 drivers, the Pay Book's Quarterly Tax card adds the year up over the IRS's own estimated-tax periods and shows what to set aside for each of the four due dates — so April never arrives as a surprise. The full story is in the Settlement Check panel right below.

Replaces: the spreadsheet, the settlement PDF folder, the end-of-week math on a napkin.
06Paperwork · Sealed + proven

Records

Paperwork that proves itself. BOLs, PODs, rate cons, logs, inspections and exports file into one Library, and every delivery seals into a hash-chained record nobody can quietly rewrite later. When the office, a broker or an officer asks, the proof is one download — not a search party.

Replaces: the filing cabinet, the photo roll of BOLs, the “which phone has that POD” hunt.
07Your rig, kept ready

Truck

Your rig, on record and kept ready. Truck and trailer identity, maintenance countdowns and the full service log, inspections and breakdown mode — a defect flagged on a walk-around drafts its own repair entry here, so nothing found at 5 a.m. gets forgotten by Friday.

Replaces: the glovebox service folder, the sticky-note mileage reminders.
08Calendar + home time

Schedule

The week, and the life around it. Your calendar, home time, and the dates that can strand you — CDL, medical card and credential expiries — watched in one place with warnings well before they become a roadside problem. The run gets planned around getting home, not instead of it.

Replaces: the wall calendar, the expiry date you meant to write down.
09Messages · Fleet + shares

Team

Everybody on the run, in the loop. Messages, the fleet board and load shares live here — dispatch sees the fleet live, drivers see their assignment whole, and a broker or shipper gets a tracking view of the lane and the ETA, never the rate.

Replaces: the check-call phone tag, the group text nobody can find later.
10Points for the work

Rewards

The work pays twice. The miles you run, the map you help keep honest and the drivers you bring in earn points from your own sealed records — earned for real work, tracked right here, in the same app that sealed the proof. No separate rewards app, no points for nothing.

Replaces: the punch-card programs and points that live in an app you never open.
Straight answers

Questions drivers & fleets ask

The short version — what STONEMILES is, who it is for, what it replaces and what it costs.

What is STONEMILES?

STONEMILES by Stonervision is one all-in-one workspace for the trucking day — 50+ tools in a single app instead of a pile of separate apps that never talk to each other: truck GPS, loads and dispatch, fuel, pay, sealed trip records and IFTA, all working off the same trip. Built by a Trucker for Truckers. Every mile, sealed.

Who is STONEMILES for?

Owner-operators, company drivers, hotshots and fleets. Drivers run the day from the cab — route, loads, hours and pay — while owners and dispatchers run the same loads from the desk in the same app. One home for the whole job, from the one-truck operation to the full fleet.

What does STONEMILES replace?

The stack of separate apps and paperwork: the GPS app, the load app, the fuel app, the pay spreadsheet, the paperwork folder and the IFTA worksheet. In STONEMILES a load, its route, its fuel, its documents and its pay all live on one sealed record — nothing gets re-typed from app to app.

How much does STONEMILES cost?

Basic is free. Gold is $9.99 a month or $99 a year, Diamond is $19.99 a month or $199 a year, and Owner is $49.99 a month or $499 a year. Locked pricing with no surprises — and a yearly price stays frozen for your year.

How do I get STONEMILES?

Create a free account at app.stonervision.io — Basic is free and runs in your browser today. The Android app is rolling out through Google Play; join the beta from this site to be first in line when your invite opens.

Is STONEMILES an ELD?

No — STONEMILES keeps your hours, logs and trip records, but it is not a certified ELD unless it is connected to a certified provider such as Samsara or Motive. Where an ELD connection is active, the certified provider's system remains the ELD of record, and the driver stays responsible for hours-of-service compliance.

On the road — updated Nov 8 · Five alert systems build

A truck GPS that does the paperwork too

Everything below is in the current approved build — routing that respects your rig, a map you can read at a glance, records nobody can quietly rewrite, and fuel math that uses the price you actually pay. The Nov 6 repair de-crowded the Drive map so speed is always visible, made fuel pins load again, kept search typing in the bar, and turned the route line green at night. The newest build adds five alert systems: runaway ramp alerts on steep descents, sharp curve and rollover alerts, railroad crossing alerts, a severe weather and winter package, and one-tap hazard reports — on top of traffic lights on the map and construction indicators drivers report and share. The Cab Mode build adds a glanceable in-app cab display and Android Auto template screens previewed in-app — see the Cab Mode section below for exactly what is built and what is still on the road to the dash. The newest build also makes the fleet dispatch chain live and adds the User Library — the full flow is laid out in the dispatch section right below. The latest builds add the Tax Worksheet inside the Library and simplify the whole app to one home per job — one dock, one Records home and one Desk. The newest build adds My Truck and My Trailer records in Settings → Truck — with photos on the driver profile — and a Maintenance log in the Money hub next to the maintenance countdown, with receipts on each entry and a Download truck record button that pulls truck identity, specs and the full log into one file. The latest builds add the three SM Points lanes — Drive well, Feed the map, Grow it — paid from your sealed records; DVIR pre-trip and post-trip inspections whose flagged defects draft their own maintenance entries; a sealed detention clock in the Money hub; and a model field on the trailer record, so the rig record reads year, make and model on the trailer too. The newest build puts inspections right into the day — Pre-trip and Post-trip buttons beside the hours-of-service clock, the pre-trip opening on its own at the first On Duty of the duty day — and stamps every duty change with a one-tap remark and the city, state and time, the way the federal log requires. That is the point of one workspace with 50+ tools: the GPS, the hours, the inspections and the log live together, so there is no separate logbook app and no inspection form to chase down later. The public demo above shows this same build with fake data.

Truck-legal turn-by-turn

Guidance built for a 13′6″ / 80,000 lb / 53 ft rig — low bridges, weight limits, and truck bans routed around, with bridge-height alerts that show the posted clearance before you get there, spoken directions, and automatic rerouting when you leave the route. By day the route line is blue; in the map’s night look it turns green so it stays easy to follow against dark roads — and the traffic legend matches the line you see.

Hill grade alerts — with your speed

Know the hill before you are on it. STONEMILES warns you in advance of steep downgrades and climbs, with your live speed right on the alert banner so you can see how fast you are rolling into it. On descents you get gear-down and brake-check prompts in time to act, and heavier rigs get their warnings earlier. While you drive, a live grade readout sits beside your speed, and it all works offline from the elevation stored with your route — no signal needed in the mountains.

Traffic lights on the map

Traffic signal locations show on the map and ahead on your route, so you can see the lights coming before you reach the intersection. The layer works offline — locations only. STONEMILES does not show live red or green timing.

Construction indicators

See a work zone? Report it with one tap and it is shared with other drivers, shown with its age. Zones expire unless re-confirmed, so old reports do not linger. Approaching one on your route triggers a banner and a voice call. Where a state DOT offers a free feed, official zones appear too — every zone is labelled by source: “Driver-reported” or “DOT reported.”

Runaway ramp alerts

On steep descents, STONEMILES calls the escape ramps ahead — before you need one. Ramp locations come from map data only, so you hear where the next runaway ramp sits while you still have time to plan for it.

Sharp curve / rollover alerts

Curve advisories are measured against your rig — your live speed, height and weight — not a car on the same road. A curve that is tight for a tall, heavy load warns before you are in it, and it works offline.

Railroad crossing alerts

Crossings ahead on your route are called in advance, with live crossing locations from OpenStreetMap. Where profile data supports it, humped crossings are flagged as high-center risks for long, low trailers — the kind a low deck can hang up on.

Severe weather + winter package

National Weather Service warnings matched to your route and your arrival time — not just where you are now. Route weather now runs the next 24 hours, hour by hour along your corridor, timed to when you will actually arrive at each point — hazards like ice, snow, storm, high gusts and low visibility called for your arrival hour, in future tense, matched to your truck’s pace. When an active requirement is posted, chain-law alerts name the chain-up pullouts ahead. Snow is called by route segment — inches expected across your next miles — with a park-it advisory at heavy accumulation. Free public data only — Open-Meteo forecasts plus National Weather Service alerts, no paid feed — and when a feed is down, the panel says so instead of inventing conditions.

Hazard reports

One tap reports what is ahead: traffic stopped, debris in the road, or a vehicle on the shoulder. Reports are shared with their age, expire in 2 hours unless re-confirmed, and are mirrored on the Cab Mode head unit so the warning reaches the big screen too.

Satellite view + tilt — de-crowded

See the yard, the dock and the interchange as they really look. Map, Satellite and Tilt now sit in one slim row above the MPH speed bubble — nothing stacks over the speed readout, so your MPH is always fully visible. Turn the enhanced view off anytime in Settings under “Enhanced map view.” The truck-legal route stays on top either way.

Atlas — 50-state reference

Every state in one offline book: weight limits, key rules and DOT contacts, state by state. Works with no signal. Reference only — it informs the driver; it does not replace the permit, the signs on the road, or the law in that state.

Sealed trip records

Every trip is hash-chained into a tamper-evident record. Change one byte and the chain breaks — and each sealed record carries a verification code anyone can check. Works without signal, too: duty changes and inspections made with no signal are captured on the device and seal automatically when the connection returns — never presented as sealed early.

Automatic IFTA trip sheets

State-line crossings are logged as you drive. At quarter-end the sheet is already done — miles per state, pay per state, ready to file.

Fuel Coach + Net-Price Planner

The pump price is not the real price. The planner ranks stops by price minus the state fuel tax where the fuel is burned, and the Coach turns your speed and idle time into dollars. In Explore, Fuel pins now load reliably — including stations the map data records as a building or an area, not just a point — so a station that exists on the ground no longer goes missing on the map. With “Auto-add stops to my route” on — in Settings → Driving, on by default — a planned route automatically gains the planner’s picks as waypoints on that route: the best fuel stop by true cost when the tank calls for it, the 30-minute break timed off your driving clock — required after 8 hours of driving, and satisfied by off duty, sleeper, or on-duty-not-driving time, so 30 minutes fueling counts — and a 10-hour rest stop placed before your drive clocks run out. Each auto-added stop is announced with a one-tap remove, and your final destination never changes. Prefer to choose your own stops? Turn the setting off in Settings → Driving and pick your own, exactly as before. Every stop and parking pick is also planned against your remaining hours-of-service clock, with a plain fit verdict — fits, tight, or won’t make it — worked out at your truck’s real pace, not a car’s. Reservations connect when a parking partner does: until then the app says plainly that reservations aren’t connected yet and never pretends a spot is held. When a partner connects, reserving happens against the clock, with the arrival window computed from your sealed duty record.

The plan thinks ex-tax, end to end. Each stop shows its pump price and its base price side by side — base price is the pump price minus the state fuel tax — with the tax effect spelled out, how many gallons to take there, and why. That is because IFTA settles the tax where the fuel is burned, not where it is bought, so the cheapest pump price is often not the cheapest fuel. The plan’s true cost — what you spend at the pump plus the IFTA settlement — is set against the naive cheapest-pump plan, and the saving is labelled an estimate. Prices are estimates with their source labelled, and a stop with no price is never ranked or costed. Tank discipline holds the whole way: never below reserve, never past capacity.

Fuel-card checks ride along with the log. Every logged purchase is checked against the truck’s recorded position; a purchase that lands far from the truck is flagged “possible mismatch — check it,” with the evidence shown. Nothing is ever declined or blocked by the check — it is a flag to look at, not a wall. And a purchase that can’t be located reads “not checked” — never a silent pass.

Loads by photo, proof by GPS

Snap the BOL or rate con and the load is added. At the dock the receiver confirms on the receive link (the QR rides on the BOL), signs on your phone, or signs the paper BOL for you to upload as the POD — and the delivery seals by GPS geofence at the receiver, proof of delivery that carries its own evidence.

ELD connections

Connect Samsara or Motive and your ELD odometer becomes the miles of record, synced read-only into your trips and sheets. The ELD hub can run a clearly-marked simulated test sync through the real sync pipeline — test data is stamped simulated and never becomes the official record. Live sync still awaits a real ELD device, and the app says so.

Federal-rulebook logs

Your logbook plays by the federal rulebook — 49 CFR 395 Appendix A — right inside the same workspace as your GPS, loads and paperwork, one of 50+ tools in one home instead of a separate logbook app to keep in sync. Stop in Driving for 5 minutes and the app prompts you with task notes — Fueling, Loading and the rest — and your pick seals On Duty with the confirmed reason. No answer in 1 minute and it seals On Duty by itself — the federal default. Off Duty and Sleeper Berth are never automatic — only you set those. And when a fleet owner corrects your log, the correction waits as pending: your original record stands until you acknowledge it, or dispute it with a note — and that dispute prints on the DOT packet, in the open.

Notification center

Alerts land in the app — messages, load offers, credential warnings and hours warnings — collected in one notification center in the app, with nothing emailed. Phone push arrives with the Android app.

Safety Academy

Short courses that keep a clean record clean — available in English and Spanish, with completions sealed to the driver's record.

Dashcam coaching — coaching, not punishment

A camera partner sends driving events — harsh braking, speeding, following distance, collisions — and each event lands as coaching. The event keeps the partner’s clip reference — the app never hosts the video — the driver notes what happened, and dispatch marks it reviewed / coached. Repeats surface as plain pattern facts — no scores.

Exoneration vault — pin it, and the proof seals

Any camera event can be pinned into the exoneration vault: the clip reference seals together with the duty timeline, GPS summary and inspection records around it into one evidence packet that stays exactly as pinned. If a ticket or a claim comes later, the proof is one file.

SM Points for verified work

100 SM Points at free signup, 1,000 when you subscribe and at every renewal — on top of points for GPS-verified driving: sealed trips, on-time deliveries, clean days. Three more lanes now pay from your sealed records — Drive well, Feed the map, and Grow it — computed by the server from the work itself. On a paying tier, points convert to $STONER when conversion opens. Free-tier points never expire and are never forfeited for staying free — your points are yours and keep stacking; converting unlocks when you upgrade.

One search — loads, drivers & paperwork

One search box at the top of Today and on both desks — “your loads, drivers & paperwork.” Results come back grouped — Loads / Drivers / Paperwork — capped, with the cap stated. Search only ever reaches your own records, and rates never appear in a result.

Drive & Explore — the verdict repair

Four fixes from real use in the cab, now in the approved build. No new claims — the same map, made readable and reliable.

1 · Speed you can always see

The Drive / Explore controls were crowding the speed readout. They are now grouped in one slim row, clear of it. The speed-limit sign now always says what it knows and never just goes blank: it shows the posted limit, holds the last known limit (labelled) on the same road while a fresh lookup runs, shows “CHECKING…” while it looks, and settles honestly to “NO LIMIT DATA” where no posted limit is on record — for example parked in a lot on unposted roads.

Fleet dispatch · Live in the newest build

Broker to sealed delivery — one chain

The fleet dispatch chain is live. A load moves from the broker to the receiver’s signature without ever leaving STONEMILES — and the moment it is signed, the delivery seals itself and lands in the Library, ready to print, email or download.

Broker sends→ Desk accepts→ Driver assigned→ Driver runs it→ Receiver confirms on the link→ The delivery seals itself→ Everything lands in the Library — printable · emailable · downloadable

Fleet owners — your desk books it, your drivers run it, the record seals itself.

STEP 1

Broker sends

The load comes in through either broker door below — pickup, drop, rate con and BOL details attached — addressed to the fleet that will run it, or posted to the loadboard.

STEP 2

Desk accepts

The fleet desk reviews the load in the fleet’s inbox and accepts it onto the board. Nothing rolls until the desk says yes.

STEP 3

Driver assigned

Dispatch assigns the load to a driver right from the fleet desk. Trucks are ranked by the real empty miles they’d drive to the pickup — a truck already under load is measured from where its current route ends. The driver gets the full load on their phone — addresses, times, paperwork and notes.

STEP 4

Driver runs it

The driver runs the load with truck-legal routing, HOS clocks and the trip sealing as they go — the desk watches the load move, not a phone tag game.

STEP 5

Receiver confirms

At the dock, the receiver confirms on the receive link, signs on the driver’s phone, or signs the paper BOL — whichever way the dock actually works. On the link, they sign two ways: type their name, or draw their signature with finger, stylus or mouse — either one signs. Damage or shortage is noted on the spot.

STEP 6

The delivery seals itself

The first confirmation closes the delivery — the other doors then just show “already confirmed,” so there are no double entries. Dispatch and the fleet owner see it flip to delivered with the signed proof attached, and an exception flag up top if damage or shortage was noted.

STEP 7

Lands in the Library

The sealed delivery, the signed POD and the load paperwork file themselves into the User Library — printable, emailable and downloadable whenever the office, the broker or an auditor needs them.

Fleet live board & outward tracking — live

The desk doesn’t just assign the load — it sees the fleet live while the load runs, and it can share that run outward without sharing the money.

Fleet live board

The fleet’s owner and dispatch seats get a live board of their own drivers: status cards with driver, truck, current lane and plain status, stops, route end + ETA, and last location with its freshness printed. Only your own fleet sees it — never another fleet, never public — and off-duty locations stay private.

Assign ranking by deadhead

When the desk assigns a load, trucks are ranked by the real empty miles they’d drive to the pickup. A truck already under load is measured from where its current route ends, so the ranking reflects the run the truck would actually make.

Suggested next load

Inside the fleet board, each driver gets ranked next-load suggestions with the reasons printed across four legs — deadhead, calendar availability, home-time, and sealed hours. A leg whose facts are missing reads “not checked” — never assumed. One tap routes into the normal offer / assign flow and every gate still runs — qualification file, home-time and dispatch mode — so an unqualified driver can be suggested and still be refused at assignment, with the plain reason. A suggestion never bypasses a check.

Tracking links for brokers & shippers

A driver or the fleet desk can create a per-load tracking link to send a broker or shipper: lane, stops, ETA, status, and the truck’s location with freshness. It ends at delivery, can be revoked anytime, and never shows the rate or any money. Check calls post themselves: load status updates are posted automatically from the load’s sealed records to its tracking page — no driver taps, every update backed by the sealed record it came from. Anything the system isn’t sure about goes to a human exception queue with the evidence attached — never guessed, never posted on a guess. The rate is never part of what goes out. The tracking page shows the paperwork stage too — received → confirmed → sent → invoiced → paid — so the broker can see the POD is in and the invoice is cut, never the rate.

Two doors for brokers

Brokers reach fleets and drivers two ways — one aimed at a single fleet, one open to the board:

Door 1 — The send door, no account

A broker with a fleet’s code or link sends a load straight into that one fleet’s desk inbox as an offered load. No account to open, nothing posted publicly — the load lands in front of the fleet it was meant for, and the desk accepts it or passes.

Door 2 — Broker accounts on the loadboard

Brokers with an account post loads to the public loadboard, where owner-operators can see them and grab the ones that fit their truck, their lane and their week. Posting is free for brokers — the claiming carrier pays the dispatch fee.

Paperwork door — every load carries its own upload link

Paperwork no longer has to chase the driver. Each load carries its own no-account paperwork link, and the broker or carrier on the other end can drop the papers straight into that load:

No account, no app — just the link

A broker or carrier opens the load’s own paperwork link and uploads the rate confirmation, BOL or POD straight into that load — no account to open, no app to install. Rate confirmation is a first-class paperwork kind, alongside BOL and POD.

The public face shows only the lane and date

The door’s public page shows only the load’s lane and date — nothing else about the load rides on it. Files are checked on the server — the claimed file type is never trusted — and the upload lands in the same paperwork pipeline as driver-filed paperwork, with the driver notified in-app when paperwork lands.

Broker identity — on file, and re-screened every tender

A broker account is more than a login. Every broker carries an identity record, and the board checks it again every time a load is tendered — not just once at sign-up.

An identity record for every broker

Each broker enters their legal business name, MC number, BMC-84 bond — carrier and expiry — and authority status as part of the flow. Bond expiry is watched like a credential, with warnings at 60, 30 and 7 days before it lapses.

Re-screened at every tender

Every tender is screened again against that record. An expired bond, a bond under the federal minimum, revoked or inactive authority, or missing fields blocks the tender — with the plain reason shown to the broker in-app, so it can be fixed instead of guessed at.

Carriers see who’s behind the load

Before a carrier takes a board load, the load carries a trust line: the broker’s legal name, MC number, bond status and expiry month, and verification status — so you know who you’re hauling for before you commit. Bond amounts are never shown to carriers.

Double-brokering is refused

A carrier who accepts a load off the board cannot re-post it. The carrier who accepts is the carrier of record — the load stays with the truck that took it.

Each broker’s own 371.3 record file

Every broker keeps their own 371.3 record file — the full record of their own loads: the parties, the dates, and the agreed rate and charges. It is visible to that broker only.

Broker payment record — how they actually pay

Before you take a board load, you can see how the broker actually pays — figured only from STONEMILES’ own sealed history: loads carried, how many were paid, and average days-to-pay, with the sample size printed so you know how much history stands behind it. Under 3 paid loads it shows the plain facts only; with no history it reads “No payment history in STONEMILES yet.” No invented scores, no letter grades, and no dollar amounts ever ride along.

Labelled for what it is. A broker’s verification status says exactly what stands behind it — “Identity on file” when the record is entered but no verification source has checked it, or checked by a verification source when one has. Until a verification source is connected, the status reads plainly: “Identity on file — verification source not connected.” Nothing is called verified that wasn’t checked.

Driver qualification files — 49 CFR 391, kept by the Desk

Every driver in a fleet gets a qualification file under 49 CFR 391 — and the Desk keeps it current, so dispatch never has to guess who is qualified to roll.

The file that keeps itself

Driver application, CDL, medical certificate, road test, employment history, annual MVR review, the annual violation record, Clearinghouse query log and training — employment history and the annual violation record are required parts of the file, not extras — with documents held in the vault and the driver’s status computed from what is actually on file and in date. The annual Clearinghouse query goes overdue after 12 months — an overdue query leaves the file incomplete. Upcoming expiries surface ahead of time — CDL, medical and MVR review — with warnings at 60, 30 and 7 days.

Dispatch won’t hand a load to an unqualified driver

Assigning or claiming a load for a driver with an expired CDL or medical, an MVR review over 12 months old, a Clearinghouse query over 12 months old, a prohibited Clearinghouse result, an incomplete file, or no file at all is refused — dispatch stays blocked while a driver’s file is incomplete — with the plain reason shown. The hold sits in the fleet’s exception queue until the file is fixed.

One tap — the audit packet, as of any date

One tap builds an as-of-date audit packet: the complete qualification file as it stood on any chosen date — the roadside and audit answer, pulled from the file itself.

Labelled for what it is. Medical status reads “on file — electronic verification not connected” until a real verification source is wired — on file is not called electronically verified. STONEMILES records the Clearinghouse queries the fleet itself ran; it never looks a driver up itself.

At the dock — three ways to sign, one sealed record

Docks already work three ways, so STONEMILES takes all three — and every one of them feeds the same sealed record:

1 · The receive link — QR on the BOL

Every BOL carries the load’s receive link as a QR code. The receiver scans it or opens the link on their own phone, confirms the delivery, signs, and notes any damage or shortage — no app, no account on their side. On that link they sign two ways: type their name, or draw their signature with finger, stylus or mouse — either one signs.

2 · Sign on the driver’s phone

No phone of their own handy? The receiver signs right on the driver’s phone screen, name under the signature, damage or shortage noted on the spot. That signature becomes the sealed POD.

3 · Paper BOL, signed and uploaded

The traditional way still works: the driver prints the BOL (the QR rides on it), the receiver signs the paper, and the driver photographs the signed BOL and uploads it as the signed POD — sealed into the same record and pushed to dispatch and the fleet owner.

Drawn or typed — the record says which. A drawn signature prints on the signed POD, above the “Received by” line, and the sealed delivery record notes how they signed — drawn or typed. A fake or broken signature image refuses the whole confirmation — nothing seals.
The receiver keeps their own copy. The second a receiver signs digitally, a “Get your copy” prompt offers three ways to keep it: by email — the signed POD lands in their inbox; by phone number — they type their number (that entry is their opt-in), and the app hands the driver’s own phone a ready text with a view-only link to the copy, which the driver sends from their own number — no separate texting service needed; or as a document — download or print the signed copy right there on the spot. The copy is the real thing: their signature, name, timestamp, load summary and any damage notes — the same sealed POD sitting in your Library.
New in the latest build · Loads → Records → Pay

Snap it. Sealed. Paid.

The paperwork chain that used to eat the end of every run — type the load in, chase the POD, build the invoice, work out what the miles actually paid — now runs off the camera. Three snaps carry a load from rate confirmation to invoice, and every step lands on the sealed record, so the proof and the pay never live in different places.

SNAP 1 · RATE-CON READER

The load fills itself in. Snap or upload the rate confirmation and STONEMILES reads it — shipper, receiver, dates, rate — and builds the load for your check-off before it seals. You confirm what’s right, fix what isn’t, and manual entry is always there if the read misses anything. No retyping a PDF by thumb in a parking lot.

SNAP 2 · POD → INVOICE

Delivered means invoiced. Snap the POD at delivery and it seals to the load it belongs to — and the invoice draft is already waiting in Pay, built from that sealed delivery. No evening at the laptop rebuilding the run from photos and memory before you can bill it.

ALWAYS · REVENUE PER MILE

Your RPM, up front. Revenue per mile sits at the top of Pay, figured from your sealed loads — the one number that tells you whether the week worked, in front of you every time you open the door, not buried in a report you have to go build.

For drivers, it is the end of data entry as a second job: the paper reads itself, the invoice drafts itself, and the per-mile truth is just there. For fleets, loads enter the system the same way every time — read from the rate con, checked off by the driver, sealed at delivery — so the desk is never chasing a missing POD before it can bill. Auto never blocks manual: if a read comes back partial, you land in the same form with what was read already filled in and the document attached.

The User Library

Everything lands in the Library

Every delivery the chain seals — and every document the work creates — files itself into one Library per user. The Library is the app’s one Records home: loads delivered, statements, fuel tax state by state, filings, uploads, sealed files, filed document copies, the document vault, tax records, the Tax Worksheet and your truck record. No folder hunting, no “which phone has that POD.” If it happened in STONEMILES, it is in the Library.

Loads delivered

Every delivered load with its sealed record and signed POD attached — the full run from broker send to receiver signature, in one file.

Statements

Settlement and pay statements as they land, kept with the loads they pay for — so a statement and its proof sit side by side.

Fuel tax, state by state

IFTA miles and fuel broken out state by state, built from the sealed trips themselves — the quarter’s fuel tax picture without the hand math.

Filings

Quarterly filings and exports, ready to hand to your preparer or file — generated from records that were sealed as you drove, not rebuilt later.

Uploads

Everything you add yourself: BOLs, rate cons, signed paper PODs, permits, scale tickets and photos — filed with the load they belong to.

Sealed files

The hash-chained records themselves, each carrying its verification code — change one byte and the chain shows it.

Certified daily logs

Each day’s log is signed by the driver who ran it. Close the day by typing your name under “I certify these entries are true and correct” — and the certification seals into the record with the day. A day that hasn’t been certified says so, plainly — nothing is backfilled, nothing is dressed up. The log an officer, an auditor or the office sees is the log the driver stood behind — one more separate logbook app the workspace throws away.

Filed document copies

Copies of the documents you filed, kept in the Library alongside the records they belong to — ready to pull up whenever the office, a broker or an auditor asks.

Document vault

Your important documents held in the same one place — no separate vault to hunt through, because the Library is where records live now.

Tax records

The year’s tax records kept with everything else, feeding straight into the Tax Worksheet below — no separate tax folder, no rebuilding the year at filing time.

Truck record — one file

One download that pulls it all together: your truck identity and specs — year, make and model — and your trailer’s year, make and model, plus the full Maintenance log, in a single file with a printable version too — ready for the office, a shop or a buyer, and filed with the rest of your records.

The officer packet, complete — the whole record in one download

The packet an officer asks for is complete. One download from the Library with everything on your record: your loads, your HOS daily logs, your DVIR inspection reports, your truck & trailer record, the maintenance log, an IFTA summary and your credentials list. Generated fresh from your records every time you pull it, with the sealed chain’s integrity verdict stamped on the cover — one file that proves the whole record, ready for an officer, an auditor, a fleet, or your own files.

  • The whole record in one file — loads, HOS daily logs, DVIRs, truck & trailer record, maintenance log and credentials, pulled together in a single download.
  • Emailed to the officer, straight from the app — send the packet to the officer right from inside STONEMILES, without leaving the stop to find a computer.
  • A proper PDF — the packet also downloads as a proper PDF, ready to print or file.
  • Unit numbers on every day — every day in the packet prints the truck and trailer unit numbers, so each day’s log names the rig it belongs to.
  • IFTA summary — an estimate, not a filing — the bundle’s IFTA summary is labelled an estimate; it is not a filing.
  • Fresh every time, verdict on the cover — built from your records at the moment you download it, and the cover stamps the sealed chain’s integrity verdict.

Tax Worksheet — the whole tax year in one view

One full-view worksheet for the tax year, assembled automatically from the records you already keep — no re-entering, no second set of books.

  • Built from your own records — Pay Book pay entries, expense records, the fuel log, and the per-diem day count from sealed trips.
  • Income in separate lanes — W-2 income and 1099 income stay in separate lanes, each with its own subtotal — never one blended total.
  • Expenses in clear sections — including DOT testing / physical, licensing & fees, software & satellite, and maintenance & repairs.
  • Per-diem, stated plainly — per-diem and unreimbursed employee expenses are owner-operator / 1099 territory; W-2 company drivers generally cannot claim them federally.
  • A record for tax prep — not tax advice — take it to your preparer as it stands. It exports like everything else in the Library: print, email or download.
  • No tax ID, ever — the worksheet never asks for or stores a tax ID.

Quarterly Tax — the 1099 year, four due dates

Nobody withholds tax from 1099 pay — the IRS collects it in four payments a year. The Pay Book's Quarterly Tax card keeps the running total, so no due date ever arrives as a surprise.

  • The IRS's own periods — Jan–Mar due Apr 15, Apr–May due Jun 15, Jun–Aug due Sep 15, Sep–Dec due Jan 15. The second period is only two months; the card uses the real periods, not calendar quarters.
  • Netted like the packet — each period nets exactly like the 1099 packet: gross − stub deductions − logged expenses − logged fuel, every dollar counted once.
  • A set-aside for every due date — self-employment tax figured at 15.3% on 92.35% of net, plus income tax at a rate you pick, so you always know what of your money is already spoken for.
  • 1099 lane only — W-2 pay never enters; its tax is withheld already. Per diem stays out too — it's non-taxable.
  • A planning estimate — not tax advice — built from your own logged records, figured before the Social Security wage cap so it errs on the safe side.
Print Email Download — every item in the Library, no exceptions.
Truck & trailer

The trailer package

Pick your trailer once and the app thinks in that trailer — its checks, its math and its risks. Five types covered, each with its own pre-trip checklist. Settings → Truck now holds both records side by side: My Truck and My Trailer.

My Truck — in Settings → Truck

Your rig on record in one place: year, make, model, unit number, engine and transmission. VIN and plate sit in the record as private, owner-only fields. Add up to 5 photos of the truck.

My Trailer — its own record

Right alongside My Truck: year, make and model, plus the trailer type and length the app already runs on. Trailer VIN and plate are private, owner-only too. Add up to 5 photos of the trailer — it gets its own row, not an afterthought.

Reefer cold-chain log

Setpoint, checks and temperature history for refrigerated loads — a continuous log you can show the receiver, sealed with the load record.

Smart trailer — position, with its freshness printed

Trailer position shows with its freshness always printed — how old the reading is sits right on it. It is never dressed up as live.

Reefer proof — logged against the load

Reefer temperature is logged against the load. An out-of-range reading alerts the driver and dispatch in-app, and the temperature log rides with the load’s records as delivery proof.

Securement calculator

Dock helper

High-wind advisory

Light, tall and empty trailers get a plain warning when wind on your route makes the rig a sail — advisory only, the call stays with the driver.

Per-trailer pre-trip checklists

Dry van doors are not reefer doors. Each trailer type carries its own checklist — reefer fuel and setpoint, flatbed securement gear, RGN pins and hydraulics — plus the systems every rig shares, now including trailer brakes & lights and fluids & leaks — signed into the DVIR flow.

DVIR — inspections built into the day

Pre-trip and Post-trip buttons sit right beside the hours-of-service clock on Drive — no hunting through menus to start the walk-around. The pre-trip opens on its own at the first On Duty of the duty day — skippable, never a hard block — and a post-trip opens when a new load starts the same day inside the same 14-hour window after a delivery. Every inspection starts where the federal pre-trip rule says it should: reviewing the last report’s open defects first. Then it is system by system — check each one, flag defects with notes, sign it — and after a pre-trip seals, the app offers Start driving, so the day runs On Duty → Pre-trip → Drive, in that order. The signed report seals into the day’s record with the time, GPS, and the truck & trailer’s identity — year, make and model on both. Flag a defect and it automatically drafts a repair entry in the maintenance log, and the defect stays open on the next inspection until the repair is marked closed — defects can’t fall through the cracks. The checklist runs 13 items now — the parking brake stands on its own, and windshield wipers are on the list. Repairs are certified by name: closing a repair on a defect takes a named certification — who certified it, and whether it was repaired or the repair wasn’t necessary — and that certification shows on the next pre-trip review, right where the next walk-around starts. No signal at the yard? The inspection is captured on the device and seals on reconnect — never shown as sealed before it is.

Every duty change carries a remark and a place

Change duty status and the remark is right there beside the status buttons — one tap: Pre-trip, Fuel, Loading, Unloading, Post-trip, Break, Personal — or your own words when the day needs them. No duty entry seals without one, and every log entry is stamped with city, state, and time at the moment of the change — the federal logging requirement, built in, not remembered and reconstructed at the end of the day. Where a place can’t be captured, the log honestly says “not recorded” instead of making one up — and even automatic changes and offline captures carry an honest system-stamped remark. One workspace, one log: no separate logbook app, no paper remarks column. And pick “Pre-trip inspection” or “Post-trip inspection” as the remark on a duty change and the inspection checklist opens automatically, right then — the remark and the walk-around are the same tap.

The 30-minute break, stated right

The break is required after 8 hours of driving — driving time, not just time on duty — and it is satisfied by off duty, sleeper, or on-duty-not-driving time. That means 30 minutes fueling counts, and the clocks credit it exactly the way the rule does — no invented violation for time the law says satisfies the break. Stops are planned against that same clock, so the break lands where it helps instead of where it strands you. It is one more job drivers used to hand to a separate hours app — handled here, inside the same 50+ tool workspace as the route, the inspections and the log.

Clocks that match your carrier

Not every carrier runs the same week, so the hours clocks follow yours. The driver — or the fleet owner, for the whole fleet at once — picks the cycle the carrier actually runs: 60 hours in 7 days, or 70 hours in 8 days — and the clocks count against that cycle, so they never overstate the hours a driver actually has. Split-sleeper, done right: a sleeper period of 7 hours or more paired with another break of 2 hours or more — 10 hours total — counts as a proper split and extends the day the way the federal rule allows. For the driver, the clock tells the truth about the week; for the company, every driver in the fleet runs on the same real schedule. One workspace, honest clocks — no separate hours app guessing at a cycle your carrier doesn’t run.

On your profile — one switch. Turn on “Show my truck & trailer on my profile” and your profile carries two photo rows: the truck line — year, make and model — with its photos, and the trailer line — year, make and model — with its photos. VIN, plate and unit number never show on the profile.
Loads & money

Know what a load really pays

The money batch from the latest build — seven tools that answer the questions drivers actually ask at the end of the week: what did I earn, who still owes me, and what is about to expire or break — now with the Maintenance log sitting next to the maintenance countdown in the Money hub.

Money Overview — your whole year in one glance

Sitting at the very top of the Money tab, above everything else: your year-to-date gross pay, what you actually kept, and the margin between them — the whole year in one glance, no digging through a pile of settlements to find it. Right under it, what you kept vs. what was taken out sits as one clear split, so every dollar of gross is accounted for. Every deduction is grouped by kind — fuel, operations, insurance, escrow, taxes withheld, and other — each with its share of the whole, so a leak can’t hide in the paperwork. Your real rate per mile is figured from your own sealed loads, and the week-by-week earnings trend shows you growing — or slipping — across the year; once there’s a month of recorded weeks behind you, a full-year pace line joins it — a pace, not a promise. For drivers, it’s their money finally readable. For owners, it’s seeing whether their drivers are actually making money — because a driver who can see his year is a driver who stays. And it all lives inside the one workspace with 50+ tools that replaces the pile of separate apps — the GPS, the loads, the hours and the money finally in one place instead of scattered across a phone full of logins. It all comes from your own recorded pay and your sealed loads — nothing recorded, nothing shown; the app never invents a number.

True rate & the Worth-It Advisor

Save your own factoring % and dispatcher % in Settings → My pay — the cuts your factoring company and dispatcher take from a load’s gross pay. The Load Worth-It Advisor takes those cuts out first, shows each one as its own line, and judges the load on what’s left after them — not on the headline rate. True Rate runs the same math after you book it: your per-mile rate net after those fees, shown next to net after fuel, on top of the real miles, deadhead, detention and time — so you compare loads on what they truly pay.

Who-owes-me board

Every unpaid load in one board — broker, amount, age and status — so nothing ages out quietly in a folder of PDFs.

Invoicing

Sitting right under Who Owes Me in the Money tab: cut a real, branded invoice from a delivered, sealed load — your business name and logo from your Business profile letterhead in Settings, the lane and the amount owed. Issue it, send the PDF, and mark it paid when the money lands — the payment is recorded and the load clears off the Who Owes Me board. The rate prints on the invoice only — never on a share link. Paperwork-to-pay: scan the BOL/POD on the load and the paperwork chases itself — once the delivery is sealed and the POD is confirmed, the POD copy sends itself to the broker/factor address on file and the invoice cuts itself off the sealed delivery, issued Net-30. The load tracks the paperwork stage by stage: received → confirmed → sent → invoiced → paid. The fields are always confirmed by the driver before anything sends — the driver confirms or corrects what the app read, and until a reading service is connected the driver checks the fields by hand. Nothing is ever guessed. At delivery, the receiver signs right on the confirmation link — by typing their name or drawing their signature — a drawn signature prints on the signed POD, the sealed record notes how they signed, and a broken or fake signature image refuses the confirmation. And every load carries its own paperwork door: the broker or carrier opens the load’s upload link — no account, no app — and drops the rate confirmation, BOL or POD straight into the load; the public page shows only the lane and date, and the driver is notified in-app when paperwork lands.

Accounting that keeps itself — QuickBooks Online & Xero

Connect QuickBooks Online or Xero once and the books keep themselves: issued invoices, recorded payments and driver settlements sync to the books on their own. Payments recorded in the books flow back through the same sealed record and mark invoices paid — never a second money path. Re-running a sync never duplicates a book entry. When both sides changed the same record, it waits in a review list with both versions shown for a person to pick — money records are never auto-merged. Until a provider is connected, the panel says so plainly.

Factoring — packaged, not pretended sent

Once an invoice is issued on a delivered load with a confirmed POD, it packages itself for factoring — the invoice and the confirmed POD assembled as one package, ready to go. With no factoring partner connected, the package stops there and says so plainly: “packaged — no factoring partner connected.” Nothing pretends it was sent. When a partner connects, submission, advance and settlement track right on the invoice, so you can see where the package stands without chasing it.

Accounts receivable — ages itself

In the Money tab, every invoice is aged by how long it has been owed, so you can see what is current and what is overdue at a glance. Factored invoices are split out on their own, so nothing double-counts, and paid totals sit alongside — all figured from your own invoice records only.

My Settlement

Sitting right under Who Owes Me in the Money tab: every sealed load with what it actually paid you, figured load by load from your own pay setting — your percent of the load’s pay, or your cents per mile. Read-only, and yours alone — each driver sees only their own loads. No guessing what a load paid.

Profit & Loss

Sitting right under My Settlement in the Money tab: what the operation actually made — income from sealed loads and claim events, against fuel, expenses and maintenance, the same lanes as the Tax Worksheet — rolled up by month, quarter or year. Your numbers only; nothing is shared.

TONU / layover logger

Truck ordered, not used — or a layover that ate your day? Log it at the moment it happens, with time and place sealed for the claim.

Document expiry wallet

License, medical card, permits, insurance and registrations with expiry warnings before they become a roadside problem — or a ticket. The three credentials you cannot roll without — your CDL, medical card and TWIC — carry a dedicated watch of their own: warnings at 60, 30 and 7 days out, plus an expired warning, so a credential never lapses by surprise. Dismiss one warning and only that round goes quiet — the next mark still fires, and a renewed card re-arms the whole watch. Those warnings land in the app’s notification center.

IFTA estimator

A running estimate through the quarter, on top of the sealed IFTA trip sheet — no quarter-end surprises, no hand math.

Maintenance countdown & breakdown mode

Countdowns to the next service by miles and days. Break down and one tap switches the app to breakdown mode: safe-stop guidance, location share for help, and the event logged to the record.

Maintenance log — next to the countdown

Every service and repair in one log in the Money hub: date, odometer, category, shop and cost, newest first with a running total. Receipts and paperwork attach to each entry and download on their own. A defect flagged on a DVIR drafts its repair entry here automatically — and stays open on the next inspection until the repair is marked closed. Download truck record pulls truck identity and specs — and the trailer’s year, make and model — plus the full log into one file — printable version included.

Fault codes — plain language, with an urgency

Fault codes — typed in by the driver or fed from the truck — are translated into plain language with an urgency: stop now / service soon / watch. The serious ones draft their own work order in the maintenance log. A code the app doesn’t know is recorded exactly as reported — never given an invented meaning. Service-due flags are figured from the truck’s own sealed readings and labelled estimates.

Detention proof — the sealed dock clock

Tap ARRIVE at the gate and DONE when the dock releases you — both stamps seal into the record with the appointment and the free time (2 hours by default). The shareable proof shows times and place only — never a rate: your own agreement prices the time, the app proves it. And time provably spent detained at the dock no longer counts against your on-time record.

Detention collection pack

That sealed proof now becomes a collection pack automatically — facility, sealed arrival and departure, appointment, total wait, free time and the time beyond it, GPS in and out, and the load reference — filed in the Library like your other documents. If you recorded detention terms on the load, the pack prices the claim from your recorded terms, labelled as yours; with no terms on file the amount line stays blank — the app never invents a rate. Claim status is tracked end to end: generated → sent → acknowledged → paid / disputed. And each facility builds a detention history from sealed visits only, with the visit count printed — a pattern is only called at 3 or more visits.

Inside Pay · New in the latest build

Settlement Check — should vs. did

A settlement statement is a claim. Your sealed loads are the evidence. Every settlement you log in Pay is checked automatically against the loads STONEMILES sealed while you ran them — no button to remember, no spreadsheet to build. The check puts the two side by side and says, in plain language, whether the money matches the work.

Should — from your sealed loads

What should have been paid

Figured load by load from the loads you actually hauled and sealed — the record that was locked in at delivery, before any statement existed. It cannot be edited after the fact to fit the check.

VS
Did — from the settlement you logged

What was paid

The settlement as it landed — the amount that actually showed up, with every deduction the statement took written out as its own line, not buried in a total.

Deductions, itemizedEach deduction on the settlement is listed on its own line and matched against the load it was taken from — so a charge with no load behind it has nowhere to hide.
Load by loadEvery sealed load in the period is accounted for — paid, short, or missing from the statement entirely. A load that never appears on the settlement is called out, not skipped.
Any shortage, flaggedIf did comes in under should, the difference is flagged right on the check — stated in plain dollars, not a code, not a percentage, not a footnote.Short — flagged in $
STEP 1

Log the settlement. When a settlement lands, record it in Pay — the amount and its deductions, as stated.

STEP 2

The check runs itself. STONEMILES lines the settlement up against your sealed loads for the same period — automatically, every time.

STEP 3

Read should vs. did. Deductions itemized, loads accounted for, and any shortage flagged in plain dollars — ready to take back to the office with the sealed proof behind it.

For drivers, it ends the quiet question at the end of every week — is this actually right? — with an answer built from records nobody rewrote. For fleets and owners, it means your drivers can check their own pay against sealed proof, so a real shortage surfaces fast and a fair settlement never gets argued on suspicion. Nothing recorded, nothing checked — the app never invents a number; it only compares yours.

On the road — extras

The details that save a day

Five extras from the latest build, each labelled honestly for what it is — and what it is not.

Coverage labelled on screen

Route-ahead severe weather

Severe weather checked along your corridor ahead, not just where you sit — now arrival-timed for the next 24 hours: the forecast for when you will be at each point, hour by hour, with hazards called for your arrival time. The app shows exactly what stretch is covered and what is not — no overselling a forecast as a guarantee. Free public data only (Open-Meteo + National Weather Service) — no paid feed.

Receiver memory — “What to expect here”

Been there before? STONEMILES remembers: gate procedure, check-in, parking notes, wait patterns and dock quirks for that receiver, ready before you arrive next time.

Scale tickets + Scales finder

CAT scale tickets sealed to the load, plus a finder for scales along your route when you need to weigh before the state does it for you.

Tax categories + per-diem counter

Expenses sorted into tax categories as you log them, and a per-diem day counter that tracks qualifying days through the year — exports your preparer can actually use.

Places — not live availability

Night parking layer

Parking places layered on the map for the end of the day, tied to your HOS clocks on paid tiers. Each pick carries a fit verdict — fits, tight, or won’t make it — computed against your remaining hours at your truck’s real pace. It shows where parking exists — it does not claim live space availability, and never presents a spot as open when it has not been reported. Reservations aren’t connected yet — the app says so plainly and never pretends a spot is held; when a parking partner connects, reserving will run against the clock, with the arrival window computed from your sealed duty record.

Now in 5 languages

The app itself — navigation, tools, checklists and settings — runs in English, Español, Português, Русский and Українська. See the dashboard section below for how the language picker works.

Navigation — simplified

One home per job. Everything listed once.

The app is cleaner, simpler and easier to navigate. No more tabs explaining mostly the same thing: every tool lives in one place, listed once, under one name. The bottom dock is Today · Drive · Loads · Money · More — one home per job — and the records, the desks and the load views have each been folded into one.

THE DOCK

Today · Drive · Loads · Money · More

One home per job: Today for the day at a glance, Drive for the road, Loads for the work, Money for pay and expenses, and More for everything else — each tool in the one place it belongs, listed once.

One simple switch

RECORDS

The Library — one Records home

One Desk for your role

No more endless scroll

The Driver tab’s extra panels sit behind labelled doors, and the More directory folds by group — counts on the headers, one open at a time. Every open section has a “Close” row at the bottom of its content, so it closes from wherever you have scrolled to, and Settings opens with only Appearance open by default. Finding any tool now takes a couple of taps — never a hunt through one long page.

Driver Calendar · Live

One calendar for the whole working life

The Driver Calendar is live — and it is the planning home. One calendar holds the whole working life instead of five different places: the loads you are committed to, home time, 34-hour resets, paydays and document expiries, all sitting on the days they actually fall.

The planning home

Committed loads, home time, 34-hour resets, paydays and document expiries — in one calendar. No checking a load board for the work, a notebook for home time, and a wallet card for a renewal date. If it shapes your week, it is on the calendar.

Week for working, month for planning

Week view is for working — the days in front of you, with the times on them. Month view is for planning — home time, resets and renewals laid out far enough ahead to plan around. And at the top, the calendar answers it plainly: “What’s my next move?” — so the next thing you owe the road is the first thing you see.

Every load lands here — whichever board it came through

Every load you are bound to lands on the calendar, whichever board it came through — the fleet desk, the send door or the public loadboard. Committed is committed, and the calendar shows it the same way no matter where the load started.

Paydays ride the calendar

Paydays ride the calendar from your fleet’s pay cycle, so the day the money is due sits alongside the work that earned it. A payday reads “expected” until the settlement is recorded paid — the calendar never calls money landed before it has.

Document expiries never sneak up

Your CDL, DOT medical card and TWIC sit on the calendar on their expiry dates — with renewal warnings ahead of them on a 60 / 30 / 7-day ladder, right in the days where you plan. A renewal shows up while there is still time to book it, not at the scale house after it lapses.

Time off that says why, not just when

A time-off request carries a type — home time, medical or doctor visit (including a DOT physical), family, personal, or a 34-hour reset — so dispatch sees why, not just when. The reason travels with the request, and the days sit on the same calendar as the loads around them.

Cab Mode · Android Auto — included in every plan

Built for the dash. Honest about the dash.

Cab Mode is included in your plan — not a separate add-on, and there is no separate Cab Mode price. Basic gets the basic version; Gold, Diamond, and Fleet / Owner get the full version.

What is Cab Mode?

Cab Mode puts STONEMILES on the truck’s own screen — the head unit — instead of a phone swinging on a mount. It is built for hotshots, commercial rigs and fleet trucks, and the new generation of cabs: a dually’s factory dash running Android Auto, or the big factory screens landing in 2027 Peterbilt and Kenworth cabs and semis.

Cab Mode fills that screen with what a load actually needs — your next turn big enough to read at a glance, your speed against the posted limit, ETA and miles left, your drive clock, truck stops, parking and weigh stations ahead, and road alerts that matter when you are hauling. And no other screen in the cab carries the load with it — a drive clock tied to your sealed trip, what to expect at the dock when you arrive, and a green route line at night. No squinting, no reaching for the phone — eyes up, hands on the wheel, load moving. Basic includes the basic cab display; Gold, Diamond, and Fleet / Owner include the full version. No separate price — it is part of the tier.

The same hill grade alerts from the Drive screen appear here too — advance warnings for steep downgrades and climbs, with your live speed on the banner and gear-down and brake-check prompts on descents, on the head-unit Guidance screen and in Road alerts, with the live grade readout beside your speed.

Construction works the same way on the head unit: when a work zone is ahead on your route, the banner and voice call are mirrored on the Cab Mode display, so the warning reaches you on the big screen without reaching for the phone. Traffic lights show as locations ahead on the route — locations only, no live signal timing.

The five new alert systems ride on the head unit too. Runaway ramp, sharp curve, railroad crossing, and severe weather & winter alerts appear in Road alerts, and hazard reports are mirrored on the Cab Mode head unit — traffic stopped, debris in the road, or a vehicle on the shoulder, shown with their age — so the warning reaches you without reaching for the phone.

Head-unit projection is not live yet — it ships through the Play Store listing.

1 · Basic version — included in Basic

The basic cab version is a glanceable cab display that strips the Drive screen down to what a driver can read in one glance — big type, no clutter, nothing that needs a tap while rolling. Four things stay in front of you:

Next turn, first

The next turn leads the screen — direction, distance and street name in the largest type on the display, with the turn after it underneath. If you only look once, you look at the right thing.

Speed vs posted limit

Your current speed sits beside the posted limit for the road you are on — the same speed readout the de-crowded Drive map protects, now paired so a glance answers “am I over?” without doing math.

ETA, always on

Arrival time and time remaining stay pinned on the display and update as traffic and reroutes change — no opening a panel, no drilling into the trip to find out when you land.

Drive clock

Time behind the wheel on this trip, counting where you can see it — so the drive clock is part of the glance, not a screen you have to go looking for at the end of the day.

The seal

What “sealed” actually means

A sealed record is not a PDF you hope nobody edits. It is a chain — and a broken chain is visible to anyone who checks.

STEP 1

The road writes the record

GPS logs the trip as it happens — route, state lines, stops, and the delivery geofence — not typed in later from memory.

STEP 2

Each record locks to the last

Every record is hashed and chained to the one before it. Edit anything, anywhere in the history, and the chain no longer verifies.

STEP 3

Anyone can verify it

Each sealed trip carries a short verification code. A broker, an auditor, or your own office can confirm the record is untouched — state-level detail only, never your private data.

SEAL · SM-7K2-9QX4

An example of the verification code format printed on every sealed trip sheet. Codes check the record's integrity — they never expose a driver's private information.

For fleets

One board for the whole fleet

An owner portal with driver profiles, a STONEMILES Board, and company chats — plus the live dispatch desk: broker loads land in your inbox, you accept and assign a driver — ranked by real deadhead to the pickup — the receiver confirms, and the sealed delivery files itself into the Library. The fleet live board shows your drivers’ status, lanes, ETAs and locations with freshness — fleet-only, with off-duty locations private — and per-load tracking links let brokers and shippers follow lane, stops, ETA, status and live location, ending at delivery, revocable anytime, never showing the rate. Status updates post automatically from the load’s sealed records — no driver taps — and anything the system isn’t sure about waits in a human exception queue with the evidence attached, never guessed. Owner, Dispatch, and Driver roles, with drivers joining only on an owner-issued code.

How it’s used: The desk books a load and assigns it to a named driver; the driver accepts, or declines with a reason that goes straight back to the desk, and the desk watches it live and can reassign at any point — one desk for driver, dispatcher, fleet owner and broker.
